prompt: A team stops an ordinary fixed-sample test at the first daily p-value below 0.05. What can be said without the full look schedule and sampling design?

options.text: The false-positive rate can exceed the nominal level; its size requires the actual design.
options.explanation: Repeated optional stopping changes the rejection event, and cumulative looks are dependent.

options.text: It remains exactly 5% regardless of stopping.
options.explanation: A single planned-look guarantee does not automatically survive optional stopping.

options.text: Treat every daily look as independent.
A true null makes false rejection impossible.
options.explanation: Sampling variation can produce rejection even when no effect exists.

workedExample: The decision is now whether any look crosses the threshold, not whether one planned analysis does. Use an appropriate sequential procedure or the original fixed plan; do not infer a universal inflation percentage from the number of looks alone.

prompt: An experiment shows a strongly unexpected allocation imbalance and one uncorrected p-value below 0.05 among many metrics. Which actions are justified? Select all that apply.

options.text: Account for the multiple opportunities to claim a win.
options.explanation: Many tested metrics create a multiple-comparison problem.

options.text: Check the pre-declared primary metric and appropriate error-control method.
options.explanation: A planned analysis distinguishes confirmatory claims from exploratory leads.

options.text: Ship solely because one metric was significant and none was worse.
options.explanation: Neither broken assignment nor uncorrected selection is repaired by an attractive dashboard.

options.text: Investigate assignment, eligibility and logging before trusting treatment results.
options.explanation: An allocation mismatch may indicate groups that differ for unintended reasons.

workedExample: Treat the allocation warning and multiple testing as separate problems. Investigate whether assignment and measurement match the design, then interpret metrics using the planned family of claims. Small percentage imbalances can be strong evidence at large sample sizes.
